subject: Re: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global

messages.subject: Re: What to do when stratum extent is smaller than global
parts:
Florian, yes, this is a concern. The available area for detections
increases less fast than the method assumes, so that the estimated
detection function falls more rapidly than does the true detection
function. You can correct for this - see pp 214-216 of the 2001 intro
distance sampling book. In your case, you would want to estimate the
e(r) function separately for each point. This can be done without too
much difficulty, but it cannot be done in Distance. So this may fall
into your category of daunting!

Steve Buckland

On 22/09/2010 08:15, Florian Weller wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have only worked with line transects so far, so this point transect
> > question has me stumped.
> >
> > Bird point counts were made in a large group of different size vegetation
> > patches, each patch containing one or more point transects, depending on
> > size. As detection numbers per patch were often low, the sensible way to
> > generate patch-level density estimates seems to be to fit a global
> > detection function to the pooled data and then post-stratify by patch.
> > However, due to the varying patch sizes, there are many patches that have
> > a total patch radius (treating them as circular for simplicity) that is
> > lower than the truncation distance that was chosen (using the p>=0.1
> > criterion) for the global detection function. To my mind, applying this
> > detection function to the patch-level data in post-stratification will
> > result in density underestimation for these small patches, as this
> > function stretches to include an area that can never include sightings in
> > these cases (being outside the physical limits of the small vegetation
> > patches).
> >
> > Is this concern justified? If no, why not? If yes, what might be an
> > appropriate way of dealing with it? Two methods came to mind:
> >
> > - use a truncation distance for the global detection function that is no
> > larger than the smallest patch radius. This seems quite restrictive.
> >
> > - as a more convoluted approach, extract the global function and manually
> > evaluate/integrate it for each patch such that it is only integrated out
> > to a distance equivalent to the patch radius. This seems daunting! :()
> >
> > Hoping someone can help with this
> > best regards
> > florian weller
